sections.b: Asked whether a man may divorce his wife "for any cause," the slogan of the school of Hillel, Jesus goes back to creation: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh, so "What God has yoked together, then, no human being should separate" (Matthew 19:6). Moses allowed divorce because of hard hearts. Matthew alone keeps an exception, "except for sexual sin" (Matthew 19:9; 5:32), which churches read differently: as allowing remarriage for the innocent party (most Protestants), as allowing separation only (Catholic teaching), or as referring to unlawful unions. Mark 10:11–12, Luke 16:18 and 1 Corinthians 7:10–11 give the rule without exception.
sections.refs: Matthew 19:3–12; Matthew 5:31–32; Mark 10:2–12; Luke 16:18; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Genesis 2:24; 1 Corinthians 7:10–16

sections.b: Answering the Sadducees, Jesus says that in the resurrection people do not marry but are like God's angels (Matthew 22:30). Since the raised no longer die, the levirate duty of raising children for a dead brother ends. Churches agree that marriage as an institution belongs to this age; Latter-day Saints teach that temple-sealed marriages continue.

common: Most churches read Matthew 19:9 as allowing divorce, at least, for adultery.
uncommon: Some scholars read porneia in 19:9 as a marriage within forbidden degrees of kinship, so the exception describes an invalid marriage, not a ground for divorce.

sections.b: In Matthew 19:9 (and 5:32) Jesus forbids divorce and remarriage "except for porneia." The word covers sexual sin of many kinds. Readers have taken it as adultery, unfaithfulness during betrothal, incestuous marriage (Leviticus 18; Acts 15:20), or sexual sin in general. Much of the difference between the churches' rules on divorce turns on this word.

When the disciples say it is better not to marry, Jesus answers that only those given it can receive this saying, and names three kinds of eunuchs: those born so, those made so by others, and those who "made themselves eunuchs because of the kingdom of heaven." Nearly all readers take the last as a figure for choosing not to marry. Origen is said to have taken it literally, and the Council of Nicaea barred self-castrated men from the clergy. The saying grounds the honor given to celibate life in Catholic and Orthodox monasticism and in Catholic clergy; Protestant churches treat it as a gift for some, never a requirement.

sections.h: The rich young man and the camel
sections.b: A young man who kept the commandments asks Jesus what good he must do for eternal life; told to sell his property, give to the poor and follow, he leaves in grief, for he owned much. Jesus says a camel could get through a needle's eye more easily than a rich person into God's kingdom, but with God anything is possible (Matthew 19:16–26). Explanations that shrink the camel (a "Needle Gate," a "rope") have no ancient support. Churches differ on whether the command was for this man alone or is a counsel of perfection for some.

uncommon: The popular story of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye has no ancient evidence.

sections.b: Jesus tells the rich young man that if he gives his goods to the poor he will have treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21), the same promise Jewish teaching made for almsgiving (Tobit 4:9; Sirach 29:11–12).

In Matthew 20:1–16 a landowner pays workers hired at the last hour the same day's wage as those who worked all day, and asks the grumblers, "Is your eye evil because I am good?" From Augustine to the Reformers and beyond, the parable has been read as a picture of grace: God's reward is a gift, not wages earned by hours. Others read it as about Israel and the Gentiles, or about God's justice for the poor.

The parable of the workers in the vineyard shows day laborers waiting in the market square to be hired and paid at sundown, as the Law required (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). A denarius was a day's wage, enough to feed a family for a day.

Jesus tells the Twelve that among them whoever wants to be first will be a slave (doulos), as the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom (lytron, the price to free a slave or captive) for many (Matthew 20:26–28).

sections.h: Son of David and David's Lord
sections.b: In Matthew 20–22 the title "Son of David" is shouted by two blind men, the crowds at the entry and the children in the temple (Matthew 20:30–31; 21:9, 15). Then Jesus asks the Pharisees how the Messiah can be David's son if David calls him "Lord" in Psalm 110:1 (Matthew 22:41–46): the Messiah is David's heir and more.

Matthew alone has two animals, a donkey and her colt, and quotes Zechariah 9:9 together with Isaiah 62:11 (Matthew 21:2–7). He leaves out Zechariah's "righteous and victorious" and keeps "gentle." The crowds' Hosanna and "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name" come from Psalm 118:25–26, and Jesus quotes the same line at the end of his temple teaching (Matthew 23:39). The whole city is "shaken" (Matthew 21:10), the verb Matthew uses again at the earthquakes of the crucifixion and resurrection.

On his arrival in Jerusalem Jesus drives out the sellers and money changers, quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, then heals the blind and lame in the temple (Matthew 21:12–17). Interpreters see protest against commerce, protest on behalf of Gentiles, or a prophetic sign of the temple's coming destruction. He leaves the temple for the last time after declaring "your house is abandoned to you, deserted" (Matthew 23:38; 24:1–2).
sections.refs: Matthew 21:12–17; Matthew 23:38; Matthew 24:1–2; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Jeremiah 22:5

sections.b: Jesus retells Isaiah's song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7): the owner plants, fences and builds a tower, but the tenants kill his slaves and his son. In Matthew the vineyard bears fruit; it is the tenants, the leaders, who are judged, and the vineyard is given to others (Matthew 21:33–43).

sections.h: "Given to a nation that yields its fruit" (Matthew 21:43)
sections.b: Only Matthew has the saying that the kingdom of God will be taken "from you" and given to a nation that yields its fruit. For centuries it was read as God rejecting the Jewish people for the Gentile church. Many scholars today, noting that the chief priests and Pharisees "understood that he meant them" (Matthew 21:45), read it as judgment on Israel's leaders, with the kingdom given to Jesus' community of Jews and Gentiles. Matthew 23:39 leaves open Jerusalem's future welcome of the Messiah.

common: The traditional church reading of Matthew 21:43 was that the kingdom passed from Israel to the Gentile church.
uncommon: Some scholars read 23:39 as a conditional promise that the Messiah will come when Jerusalem blesses him.

sections.b: Asked whether it is permitted to pay the head tax to Caesar, Jesus asks whose image is on the denarius and answers, "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God" (Matthew 22:15–22). The tax had sparked Judas the Galilean's revolt in AD 6. Since humans bear God's image (Genesis 1:27), many readers from Tertullian on have taken the saying to mean that the whole person belongs to God, and Caesar's claim stops short of worship and conscience.

sections.h: The emperor's image on the coin
sections.b: The denarius Jesus asked for bore the image of Tiberius and called him son of the divine Augustus (Matthew 22:19–21). Jewish coins of the time avoided human images.

The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, tell of a woman married to seven brothers under the levirate law. Jesus answers that in the resurrection people do not marry but are like God's angels, and argues from Exodus 3:6 that God, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, is God of the living (Matthew 22:23–33). The rabbis later found the resurrection in the Torah in similar ways (Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b).
The Sadducees use the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25:5–10 to mock belief in resurrection, with a story of seven brothers that recalls Sarah's seven husbands in Tobit 3:8 (Matthew 22:23–28).

Asked which commandment is great, Jesus quotes the Shema's command to love God with all one's heart, being and mind (Deuteronomy 6:5), and joins it with Leviticus 19:18: the whole law and the Prophets hang on these two (Matthew 22:34–40). In Matthew 23:5 he criticizes widening the phylacteries (tefillin), which hold the Shema.

sections.h: The second commandment, like the first
sections.b: Jesus names Leviticus 19:18 alongside Deuteronomy 6:5 as the two commandments on which all Scripture hangs (Matthew 22:39–40), and adds it to the commandments he lists for the rich young man (Matthew 19:19). Hillel and Rabbi Akiva also summed up the Torah by love of neighbor.

Matthew 23 tells the crowds and disciples to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach from "Moses' seat" but not to imitate them, and then pronounces seven woes on them as hypocrites. Many scholars read its sharpness in light of the conflict between Matthew's Jewish-Christian community and the synagogue leadership after AD 70. Rabbinic texts also criticize hypocritical "Pharisees" (Talmud, Sotah 22b). See the chapter page for Matthew 23 on the chapter's later misuse.
Jesus criticizes those who "make their tassels bigger" to be seen (Matthew 23:5); he does not reject the custom, which he kept (Matthew 9:20; 14:36).

sections.h: Oaths by the temple and the altar
sections.b: Jesus mocks rules that treated an oath "by the sanctuary" or "by the altar" as nothing, but one by its gold or its offering as binding: every oath is finally sworn by God (Matthew 23:16–22; compare 5:33–37). The Mishnah discusses such formulas (Nedarim 1:3; Shevuot 4:13).
Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees tithe garden herbs but neglect "justice, mercy and faithfulness"; they should do both (Matthew 23:23; Luke 11:42).

Matthew 23:25–28 turns two purity rules into pictures of the heart: cleaning the outside of a cup while the inside is full of greed, and graves whitewashed so pilgrims would avoid corpse impurity, though full of bones within.

Matthew names him "Zechariah son of Berechiah," the father of the prophet Zechariah (Zechariah 1:1), though the murder between the sanctuary and the altar matches Zechariah son of Jehoiada (2 Chronicles 24:20–22). Explanations include confusion of the two, a later scribal addition, or a reference to Zechariah son of Baris, killed in the temple in AD 67–68 (Josephus, War 4.334–344). Luke 11:51 has no father's name.

Jesus warns that his own messengers will be killed, crucified and whipped in synagogues, and that the blood of all the righteous, from Abel to Zechariah, will come on that generation (Matthew 23:34–36).

The crowds greet Jesus with Psalm 118:25–26 ("Hosanna," "Blessed is the one who comes"), the children repeat it in the temple, and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22–23 about the rejected stone and Psalm 118:26 again in his lament (Matthew 21:9, 15, 42; 23:39).
Jesus' question about Psalm 110:1 (Matthew 22:41–46) assumes the promise that the Messiah would be David's son (2 Samuel 7:12–16) and shows that he is also David's Lord.

The wedding-feast parable ends: "For the called are many, but the chosen are few" (Matthew 22:14). "Called" means invited; "chosen" those found fit. Calvinist readers have heard God's choice in it, Arminian readers human response to the invitation.
Jesus promises the Twelve that in the renewal of the world they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30), a sign of Israel's restoration.

In Matthew 22:1–14 the kingdom is like a king's wedding for his son; the invited refuse, the hall is filled with others, and a guest without wedding clothes is put out. The image of the son's wedding anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9).

Jesus' words about the children, "do not stop them from coming to me" (Matthew 19:14), are read at infant baptisms in many churches, while Baptists note that Jesus blessed the children without baptizing them. John's baptism is also the subject of Jesus' question to the temple leaders (Matthew 21:25).

Jesus tells his followers not to be called Rabbi, father or leader, for they have one Teacher, one Father and one Leader (Matthew 23:8–10). Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican Christians call priests "Father" as spiritual fathers; Quakers and others avoid such titles.
